concept.name: Latency arbitrage
concept.definition: A high-frequency strategy that exploits the mechanical arbitrage opportunities created when correlated securities' prices update at slightly different times across venues, racing to trade on a stale quote before its owner can update it. Budish, Cramton and Shim (2015) show this arms race is built into the continuous limit order book design itself.
concept.intuition: When the E-mini jumps in Chicago, the SPY quote in New York is wrong for a few milliseconds; being first to pick off that stale quote is worth millions a year, so firms spend hundreds of millions on being microseconds faster.
concept.mechanics: Colocate near exchange matching engines, consume direct feeds, and send orders against quotes that have not yet incorporated price moves in correlated instruments. BCS document ES-SPY correlation falling to about 0.09 at 10 milliseconds and 0.007 at 1 millisecond, with the median arbitrage duration shrinking from 97ms in 2005 to 7ms in 2011 while profit per opportunity stayed roughly constant.
concept.formula: Median ES-SPY arbitrage profit approx. 0.08 index points per unit, about 1,000 opportunities per day (roughly $75 million per year) in the BCS 2005-2011 sample.
concept.failure_modes: The rent is competed away in speed rather than in price: as rivals get faster, capture requires ever-larger infrastructure spending for the same prize, and market-design changes such as frequent batch auctions or speed bumps can eliminate the opportunity set outright.
concept.misconceptions: That latency arbitrage involves predicting prices; it exploits purely mechanical, publicly visible mispricings whose existence depends on serial processing in continuous markets, not on information or forecasting skill.
concept.example: At 1:51:39.590 pm the E-mini jumps about 2.5 index points while SPY has not yet reacted; the fastest firm buys SPY at the stale offer and unwinds moments later at the corrected price, capturing the spread (BCS Figure 1.1 example).

citations.source: Budish, Cramton & Shim, 'The High-Frequency Trading Arms Race: Frequent Batch Auctions as a Market Design Response' (NBER version; published QJE 2015)
